result:
Rain taps against the window like a language just beyond translation. I watch it blur the streetlights into hazy gold orbs, smearing the world into something softer, quieter. There’s a particular comfort in being inside while the sky unravels—dry socks, a steaming mug of tea too hot to sip, the weight of a worn blanket across my lap. The city doesn’t stop, but it slows, as if everyone else has also surrendered to the rhythm of falling water.

I used to resent rainy days—soggy shoes, canceled plans, the grayness that seeped into my bones. But age, or maybe just time, has taught me the value of stillness. Rain forces a pause, an involuntary breath. It’s in these moments that thoughts surface unbidden: memories long shelved, half-formed ideas, questions I’ve been too busy to ask myself.

Outside, a delivery cyclist pedals through a puddle, sending up a silver spray. A couple dashes under a shared umbrella, laughing at their near-miss with a gutter stream. Life persists, just differently. Rain doesn’t erase the world—it reframes it. It reveals reflections in pavement, the slick shine of leaves, the way light bends through droplets like tiny prisms.

I take a cautious sip of tea. The warmth spreads through my chest. Somewhere, someone is singing in the shower; another is writing a letter they may never send. Rain connects us in its quiet way, this shared, dripping pause in the relentless forward march. And for now, that’s enough. Just this: rain, tea, the hum of the fridge, and the luxury of doing nothing while the world washes itself clean.
